overview: Cassander, also spelled Kassander, took control of Macedonia after Alexander the Great’s empire fragmented. He was master of Macedon from 316 BCE and adopted the royal title around 305 BCE. The imported map record runs from 300 to 200 BCE, but he died in 297 BCE: most of that displayed interval belongs to later rulers, not his kingdom.

periods.title: Cassander’s control of Macedonia
periods.summary: A successor of Alexander consolidated power and became king.

items.text: Cassander married Alexander’s half-sister Thessalonike and rebuilt Thebes, but his consolidation of power was also violent. He had the young Alexander IV killed around 310 BCE, removing Alexander the Great’s son from the struggle for the throne.

He established two major cities in strategic coastal positions: Cassandreia took his own name, while Thessaloniki took his wife’s. A city’s name could advertise a royal family almost as effectively as a coin.

Thessaloniki’s foundation in 316/5 BCE brought together inhabitants from 26 surrounding townships. Building a new royal city meant moving people as well as laying out streets. The city’s later importance grew from this deliberate concentration of population around the Thermaic Gulf.

Pella expanded northward in Cassander’s time. Its Hellenistic plan arranged buildings in regular blocks between straight streets, with a broad route through the centre. Planning a capital meant organising movement between the harbour, market and palace.

The Hellenistic city had clay water pipes and large masonry drains with openings for cleaning. Water had to arrive, and wastewater had to leave. Those maintenance openings are a reminder that ancient plumbing needed somebody willing to do the unpleasant jobs.

Pella’s houses commonly centred on courtyards, sometimes surrounded by colonnades. Rich households decorated dining rooms with mosaics; smaller houses might have just one broad porch. Surviving grand residences should not be mistaken for everybody’s address.

The House of Dionysus has pebble mosaics dated 325 to 300 BCE, including Dionysus riding a panther and a lion hunt. These floors belong to the generation of Cassander’s rise. Dinner guests had dramatic scenes beneath their feet.

At the palace, a swimming pool, dressing room and adjoining bath were built near the end of the fourth century BCE. Excavated pottery and coins help establish the date. The researchers identify this bathing suite as royal: the king’s swimming arrangements were not a public pool for the whole city.

A small terracotta figure of sleeping Eros came from a child’s burial in Pella’s eastern cemetery and is dated 325 to 300 BCE. This quiet object brings a child into a history so often dominated by adult rulers and battles. Its burial context is known; the child’s personal story is not.

A bronze coin dated about 305 to 297 BCE carries the Greek words ΚΑΣΣΑΝΔΡΟΥ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ, “of King Cassander”. This is the museum’s transcription of the ancient inscription, not a phrase invented for the card. Even a small coin could announce who claimed to rule.

The same coin shows Heracles wearing a lion skin on one side and a young rider on the other. Cassander placed his own name beside familiar heroic and equestrian imagery. Royal messages travelled on objects people could hold in one hand.

A recorded inscription from Cassandreia confirms land for Perdikkas, son of Koinos, including property previously allotted to his father and grandfather. The grant made ownership hereditary and allowed descendants to exchange or sell it. Family advantage could be written into royal decisions.

That grant also exempted Perdikkas and his descendants from taxes on imports and exports connected with the property. It is a glimpse of unequal economic privilege: one favoured household received written advantages that should not be assumed for every farmer.

ending.text: Cassander died in 297 BCE. Quarrels among his heirs soon destabilised Macedonia, which continued under other rulers. His personal kingdom therefore ended long before the imported map’s 200 BCE endpoint, while his new cities outlasted the dynasty.
